claims.text: The initial PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles are uniform solid solutions with a near-equiatomic composition.
Increasing the relative Pt content increases the density of Pt-rich surface ensembles.
Increasing Pt content changes the distribution of surface ensembles.
Pt-rich surface sites favor optimal adsorption of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Increased Pt content modifies the local electronic environment at the catalyst surface.
Increased Pt content modifies the local atomic arrangement at the catalyst surface.
The Pt-induced surface changes reduce the binding energies of poisoning intermediates.
Reduced binding of poisoning intermediates enables more effective catalytic turnover during ethanol oxidation.
Increasing Pt content will increase ethanol-oxidation catalytic activity relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Increasing Pt content will improve selectivity for desirable products relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Increasing Pt content will improve durability relative to the equiatomic baseline.
The proposed relationships apply to nanoscale catalysts under electrochemical ethanol-oxidation conditions between 300 and 500 K.
Particle size, support interactions, and operational parameters are to be controlled when testing the hypothesis.
The experimental baseline is an equiatomic Pt-Pd-Rh-Ru-Ir-Os catalyst.
The proposed catalyst series spans approximately 16.7 at.% to 30 at.% Pt while preserving the relative proportions of the other five elements.

contradictions.description: The intervention says Pt concentration increases while the other elemental fractions remain constant, which is impossible for normalized atomic fractions. The experimental design instead says the relative amounts of the other elements remain constant, implying that each of their absolute fractions decreases.
